speechtext: ON 1955-56 crop

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to advise the house that there will be an interim payment on the 1955-56 pool account for wheat. The payment decided upon will be 10 cents per bushel on all grades of wheat, except milling grades of Durum wheat. On milling grades of Durum wheat the interim payment will be 25 cents per bushel.
In reaching this decision in regard to an interim payment, the government has been guided by a statement of the position of the 1955-56 wheat account, as prepared by the Canadian wheat board. This statement indicates that the selling of wheat in the pool is well advanced and the account is in a surplus position on all grades of wheat delivered to the board by producers between August 1, 1955 and July 31, 1956. These deliveries amounted to 352.2 million bushels. The extent of the interim payment is based upon the recommendation of the wheat board.
The interim payment will provide for the distribution of approximately $37,300,000 to producers who delivered wheat to the pool in the year ending July 31 last.
In its main features, the interim payment which I am announcing is similar to the interim payment on the 1954-55 pool which I announced in the house on February 2, 1956, except that it is larger. The main difference is that, in the case of the 1955-56 pool, the interim payment of 10 cents per bushel will apply to all grades of wheat with the exception of milling grades of Durums; whereas in the case of the 1954-55 pool an interim payment was not possible on No. 5, No. 6 and feed wheat and some other grades. On some grades the interim payment a year ago was 5 cents per bushel.
I expect that the wheat board will be able to commence issuing interim payment cheques from the 1955-56 pool on about the same date as a year ago; the actual mailing of cheques to producers will commence about the middle of February or shortly thereafter.
It is not possible, of course, at this time to state definitely when the final payment will be made on the 1955-56 crop but on the basis of the information now available it would appear that an announcement of a final payment should be possible at about the same date as last year, during next May.

DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS Loans, investments and advances-
545. Loan to the United Nations Organization to help finance the clearing of the Suez canal. $1,000,000.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO INTRODUCTION OF FURTHER LEGISLATION
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, last evening the Minister of Finance said that later in the discussion he would give a detailed explanation of this item and would discuss it at length; at least this is what I gathered from the remarks which were reported in Hansard. He said he would make a brief explanation, and give a more detailed one later if it was desirable.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO INTRODUCTION OF FURTHER LEGISLATION
speechtext: Read what I said about that at the conclusion of the session.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO INTRODUCTION OF FURTHER LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Well, I have read the entire statement, and I think that the suggestion which was made by the minister at the beginning of his remarks was very proper, and that the house and the country deserve a better and more complete summary as to the reasons for this loan. After all, it brings into focus a number of questions of paramount interest at this time for the preservation of peace in the Middle East and, indeed, throughout the world, and I have a number of questions which I wish to ask the minister.
Is the loan going to be effective, in the opinion of the minister, in providing for the opening of the Suez canal? What assurance is there that if the canal is opened Nasser, who up to now has defied every order made by the United Nations, will allow free passage for the ships of all countries, including Israel? What are the provisions for repayment? What has the minister to say with regard to the apportionment of responsibility for the destruction which has been done to the canal? Will Nasser be required to pay for the damage which, after all, was mainly, if not entirely, caused by him, and voluntarily done? I think we ought also to know how an allocation was arrived at whereby Canada assumes a disproportionate share of the actual amount to be lent to the United Nations.
These are matters which are being discussed today in the United Nations. Indeed, as one looks back over the last two or three months, one can only conclude that in the sorry history of the situation in Suez this loan would never have been required had there not been vacillation and uncertainty on the part of the free world-an attitude which has had the result of elevating Nasser to a prominent position as the dictator of the Middle East, and as the predeterminator, according to his will and his whim, of the orders made by the United Nations.
All these things arise under this section. But as yet, the house has not been made aware of the stand which is being taken by Canada at the United Nations, or respecting the direction or order made by the United Nations requiring Israel immediately to evacuate the entire Gaza area as well as the area in the vicinity of the Gulf of Aqaba.
On June 19, the secretary general was instructed to make, within five days, a report as to whether or not Israel would withdraw to the armistice line and, strangely enough, the secretary general has interpreted his mandate as giving him no right to demand or provide guarantees which Israel is seeking before evacuating the small areas she now occupies-the greater portion of the areas occupied having long since been evacuated by Israel. I think we have the right to know what attitude Canada is taking in this regard.
Israel has asked for guarantees to prevent Egypt from resuming raids on her territory, and to end the blockade that is imposed by Egypt in direct contravention of the orders of the security council promulgated in 1951. The secretary general says that nothing can be done by the United Nations to provide a strong force, except by the consent of Egypt. Surely this house and the country have a

Supply-External Affairs right to know how long this system of blackmail by Nasser will be permitted to continue. He has been allowed to say what the conditions governing the force shall be; he has been allowed to determine the tenure of that force; he has taken it upon himself to say that when, in his opinion, the emergency force should be withdrawn, that force shall be withdrawn. And in the last three or four days he has made his threat that unless the Israelis leave the Gaza area unconditionally he will, or may, make the canal unusable; and that he may find it necessary to call in the so-called Russian volunteers.
Sir, what assurance have we that if the canal is cleared Nasser is going to resume the responsibility of a nation enjoying membership in the United Nations? You say: What connection has the emergency force with a loan to clear the canal? There can be no peace, no permanence, brought about by the clearing of the canal unless before it is done responsibility is accepted by Egypt for a discontinuance of its previous wrongful acts.
I ask the minister to set out in detail what plans the United Nations has, what stand our representative, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, is taking on behalf of Canada, in order to assure that the United Nations will have its directives respected not only by Israel but also by the grave wrongdoer, Nasser, who has treated the orders of the United Nations as so many scraps of paper. This week the United Nations faces its greatest challenge. It will either go forward to new strength or it will be emasculated in the same manner in which the league of nations was destroyed by similar action and defiance by Mussolini.
Would the minister say whether or not in Canada's opinion the Israelis should unconditionally withdraw from the Gaza area before the United Nations emergency force marches in in order to prevent a repetition of the border raids and the guerrilla attacks that have continued for seven years? Unless the emergency force is accepted as an instrument that can be used anywhere to secure and maintain compliance with the United Nations directives, then it is simply a nebulous force devoid of capacity to act and totally unable to assure that the clearance of the canal will be continued and that the canal will be made open without any restrictions to the ships of all nations.
I ask the minister whether Canada has demanded in the United Nations or intends to demand that when the Israelis evacuate their points of occupation on the gulf of Aqaba the Egyptian blockade of Israeli ships will end and all nations will be assured of equality of opportunity to utilize the canal and its
[Mr. Diefenbaker.I

facilities. Sir, if the canal is to be cleared by the United Nations through loans provided by member countries within the United Nations, have we not the right to be assured that Nasser's sole control of the canal shall end? Otherwise this is just a stopgap, another act of appeasement to Nasser.
Remember that he has said that if at any time he does not wish to maintain the canal as an open waterway he has the right to say so. I doubt whether in the last century there has ever been an equal defiance of the conscience and will of the free world than has taken place in the last few weeks. When parliament is asked to vote for a loan we have a right to know the degree to which, in the opinion of those in the government with a full knowledge of the subject, the clearing of the canal will effectually assure freedom of ingress and egress to all nations. If the United Nations allows Egypt this week to flout its authority Nasser will have been established on an eminence as a dictator in the Middle East. The future will then be fraught with fear and foreboding and the U.S.S.R. will have used him as a pawn to bring about that which they have endeavoured to achieve for more than 300 years, namely, a control over the Middle East that until now has been denied them.
Nasser has become emboldened by the unconditional support he has received from the general assembly, and I ask the minister if the Israelis withdraw from these two strategic points, Gaza and the gulf, there will be assurances that in so far as Canada's representative at the United Nations is concerned every precaution will be taken to assure that the United Nations emergency force will occupy these two areas and prevent aggression on the part of Egypt in the gulf area and in the Gaza area-prevent aggression on the part of Arab terrorists as well as prevent any bands from Israel from attacking or raiding in that area. Certainly the situation seems most anomalous in that Nasser, having defied the United Nations over and over again, having refused to obey an order made in 1951 to assure that the canal should be open and that Israeli ships should have freedom to pass through the canal, now insists, as one who has himself defaulted, that the state of Israel, the last bastion of freedom in the Middle East, shall be divested of all hope of protecting itself.
I ask the minister this. What assurances have we that when the canal is cleared Nasser, who up to now has adopted an attitude of international brigandage, will become a law-abiding member of the United Nations and will assure all nations complete freedom in the use of the Suez canal?

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO INTRODUCTION OF FURTHER LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there are a few things I should like to say on the supplementary item now before us and I hope to deal strictly with the matter of the Suez canal itself. The Minister of Finance is asking the house for its authorization of a loan of $1 million for the clearance of the Suez canal. On the surface, and I think I can say almost fundamentally, we are in favour of the loan, but naturally a number of questions should be asked and answered before authorization is given.
The situation is very similar to what would exist if I approached you, Mr. Chairman, or any other member of the house and asked for a loan to rebuild a house that had been partially destroyed by fire. Naturally you would like to know how the building was going to be used and administered. We as members of the House of Commons are in the same position in asking questions on this estimate authorizing the granting of a loan. We all agree that the Suez canal must be cleared and reopened for all ship traffic, but when the government asks for authorization of a loan of $1 million then before such authorization is given we ask the government to give as full information as they possibly can on what their stand, position and policy are regarding the Suez canal once it has been cleared. As I said a moment ago, Mr. Chairman, if I were to ask you for a loan to rebuild a house or other building you would hesitate very much to lend me the money unless you knew the purpose for which the building was going to be used. You would hesitate very much unless you knew. You would not want it to be used as a bootlegging establishment, a house of ill fame or something not in the best interests of the community. The same thing applies with regard to the Suez canal, which is of such vital importance to all the world. When this government is asking us to authorize a loan for its clearance we should know the attitude of the government on the use that is going to be made of it once it is cleared.
I agree with a great many of the indications that have just been given by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) with regard to Colonel Nasser himself. In my own humble estimation there is no question whatsoever that he has been overcome by his own verbosity, that he thinks he is now the rising, shining light of the Arab world and that he is developing an attitude-and one expressed in words-which is similar to that which was evident during the rise of Hitler in Germany. Hitler in Germany and Mussolini in Italy cost the democratic world a great deal in money and in lives. We cannot see it happen again. Now, when it is 82715-51J
Supply-External Affairs in the embryonic stage, is the time for democratic countries in parliaments like ours to make our opinions known.
We in this group definitely are of the opinion that, as members of the United Nations, as one that is making a major contribution in the emergency force and one that is now being asked to make a loan for the clearance of the canal, this country through its government should at this time announce its view on its operation once it is cleared. I think it is only logical and reasonable to believe and to say that a waterway such as the Suez, canal, which is important to the entire world,, cannot be left under the domination and' subject to the whims of a would-be dictator or of one country. Surely it is reasonable-and logical, having the future in mind, to-ask the government whether, in asking for: this loan and in view of the other expenditures that this government is obliged to make, they are prepared to state that in the United Nations they are either going to put forward or support international control of an international waterway as is the Suez canal.
As the situation is at the present time, the only way in which it is possible to have international control of an international waterway such as the Suez canal is under the aegis of the United Nations. Hence the first question we should like to ask in considering the supplementary estimates is whether that is the attitude of the government and whether they will press it with everything they have in the United Nations and, in so doing, of course, give a guarantee that no country is going to be discriminated against. I would think it is obvious to all that in the re-opening of the Suez canal we cannot rely on the word of Nasser or on the word of Egypt as we have known them for quite a while past. They have indicated already over a period of five years that if they have viciousness against a certain country, they will use their control of the canal to block that country.
It was my privilege a few years ago, Mr. Chairman, to visit the state of Israel. I want to say that it was not only a pleasure but an inspiration in the time that I spent there to see a people dedicated to building a new country out of rock and sand, and they were doing it. In my estimation Israel today is the only democratic bulwark in that part of the world. It is therefore our responsibility and that of the United Nations to aid and to assist them. When in their great work, with their great objectives, they are blocked by the viciousness and dictatorship of one country, because of the Suez canal, I say that is an indication as to what some country or what some individual or persons like him would do

The Suez canal is of such great importance that such a situation has been protracted too long as far as Israel is concerned. We cannot possibly put any country in the position of facing a similar danger in the future. I speak as one who has been in that part of the world and as one who I think realizes the importance of national waterways. That is why we ask, through you, the Minister of Finance, the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Prime Minister whether, in asking for authorization for a loan at this time, they will give us a guarantee-as I hope they will-or at least an indication of the position that the government is going to take on the internationalization of the operation and administration of the Suez canal and whether a demand will be made by this government that it shall be such that no country shall be discriminated against in its trading and international affairs because of the whim of a man, a government or one country. I am certain that if we can have some indication from the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance or the Secretary of State for External Affairs on this matter, he will find that it will be accorded a great reception in this country -and that it will give the leadership required at this time in the United Nations on a matter of great importance.
We certainly support the objective, the purpose, of this loan but we feel that this information is important and imperative.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO INTRODUCTION OF FURTHER LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this item we now have before us in the supplementary estimates calls to mind, of course, the whole tragic and humiliating history of the Suez problem, beginning possibly with the seizure by Egypt of this important waterway in violation of its treaty obligations. In fact, we could say that this tragic history goes back prior to that time when Egypt deliberately refused to fulfil its obligations in allowing passage of vessels of all nations through that canal. There are those who gloss over or even support the action by Egypt in nationalizing the Suez canal. They say she was in fact justified in taking over a canal located within the bounds of Egypt. But the fact remains that the treaty that was signed does not expire for approximately two years more. The action that was entered into at that time was in direct violation of that agreement.
I am sure we are all aware of the importance of this waterway to the economy of western Europe. I understand that approximately a half of the oil supplies of western Europe find their way through the Suez canal. The canal has been called the lifeline


or the jugular vein of the economy of western Europe. I may say that the effects of the stoppage of the oil shipments were felt in France within a very few days after the canal was closed. Some of us had the opportunity of attending the NATO parliamentary conference, and we wondered just why it was that our hotel rooms were as cold as they were. Those who had a little time to spare and could not find other ways of occupying that time would remain in their rooms but they found they were too cold. Upon inquiring we were advised by the management of the hotel that oil was in short supply. They had placed their order as usual but had only received about 50 per cent of their regular supply. Rationing was going into effect and many homes were altogether without fuel. The people in that section were facing a very dreary and difficult period because of the stoppage of oil supplies through Suez.
I would suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the disgraceful display of bad temper, recrimination and retaliation over this situation has done nothing to establish confidence and goodwill amongst the nations of the free world. I would suggest, rather, that it has shaken the foundations of the free world in a very severe manner. We can understand how a situation like this could bring even the allies to a position where there are serious differences of opinion separating them. I was interested in reading a statement by the former president of the United States, Mr. Truman. In analysing the situation he said that interest in our own interests and in the interests of peace in the world should dictate that we never again allow ourselves to become separated from our allies.
There are many different phases that we must look at in connection with this particular item in our estimates, an item of $1 million to assist in the work of clearing the Suez canal. I say that before we even go that far there should be, as other speakers have suggested, some consideration given to the future status and use of that important waterway. Is the future use going to be dependent upon the whims of this sawdust Caesar as he has been called who, though defeated and discredited, has emerged as a god before whom Mr. Hammarskjold and the United Nations are bowing. A very interesting article appears in Saturday Night of January 5 with reference to this matter. Speaking of Mr. Hammarskjold it says:
. . . Dag Hammarskjold, who has found the greasy Nasser too slippery for him. But Hammarskjold, although giving an appearance of dickering with the Egyptian dictator, has really been more of a messenger boy running between United States and Cairo.

A little farther down the article states:
Nasser, with the compliance of Hammarskjold (who referred to British crews of salvage vessels, as "enemy aliens") and the U.N., has managed to make low comedy of the Canadian resolution.
They are speaking now of the emergency force.
It is intolerable that a defeated and discredited dictator can impose conditions on an international police force. If he gets away with it (and so far he has), the UNEF idea is as dead as a pickled herring.
Possibly these are very strong words, Mr. Chairman, but I would suggest there may be more than a little truth in that article. I would suggest there must be a recognition of certain very important facts in a discussion of this matter. There is more to it than just an item in the estimates. I would suggest that the whole Middle East situation is tied up in a very real way with this action that is now proposed in clearing the canal.
The question of control has been raised. Who is going to control the canal after it is cleared? Prior to the nationalization of the canal it was operated by the Suez canal company. Then, Mr. Nasser got peeved and retaliated by taking over the canal and saying he was going to use it and operate it in the interests of Egypt. After the clearance of the canal, who is going to operate it? Mr. Nasser said he may find it necessary even now, unless his conditions are met, to halt the clearing operations. Apparently the United Nations, and some of our governments who are giving such complete support to the United Nations in this matter, are willing to let him dictate the terms. Whoever operates the canal, I would suggest that there must be a guarantee of the freedom of navigation for ships of all nations. This clause was in the agreement which was violated by Egypt in the refusal to allow passage of Israeli ships.
I recall back in the fall of 1954, when I had the privilege of being at the United Nations, a particular incident was under consideration at that time known as the Bat Galin incident. It was a matter of considerable concern at that time, but the principle involved was that the Egyptian authorities refused passage to Israeli vessels and on this occasion took possession of one. I would suggest as well that some attention should be given to the Soviet-Egyptian intentions. When I was speaking a few days ago I referred to an article written by James Cromwell, former United States minister to Canada. With reference to this particular matter of Soviet intentions, he had this to say:
The president was in a tough spot because of the elections. Sir Anthony's handling of the far eastern situation has been of the utmost value to
Supply-External Affairs all free countries. The British and French uncovered, captured and destroyed millions of dollars worth of top Russian war material, stockpiled in the east.
In doing this they blocked Russia's program for conquest in the Middle East. They also revealed to the world Russian plans to gain control in the east.
I know many here will not agree with the reference to Sir Anthony Eden. I was not stressing that particular aspect at this time, but the indication by Mr. Cromwell that that action did reveal the extent of Soviet intentions and plans in that area.
Then, we should like to ask the question, where do we go from here? Has that danger been completely destroyed; has it evaporated or are we still faced with that same serious problem?
I should like to refer to Newsweek magazine of January 14, 1957 where on page 16 under the heading "Danger Signals" I read:
East Berlin-The word here is that Egypt's President Nasser soon will send a delegation to Czechoslovakia to arrange for a second big arms shipment, including tanks, armored cars, and spare parts. In addition, 500 Egyptian army officers will arrive around February 1 to train in heavy-tank operation and jet-fighters and bombers.
Reports in the newspapers these last few evenings have referred to the continued supply of Russian materials to those countries in the Middle East. What is going to happen? Is any thought at all being given to this matter? What action is being taken? What safeguards are being provided? I think these questions are also of importance when we are considering an item like the one which is presently before us.
There are other problems to be considered. There is the problem in relation to the gulf of Aqaba, border guarantees and the United Nations emergency force. But over and above all of these hovers the great problem of the political settlement of the entire Middle East situation. We should not forget that these are what might be described as minor aspects of the over-all problem of the Middle East and if we cannot find a solution to the major problem the others will not amount to much.
With regard to the policy of the United Nations I believe I speak for a great many Canadians when I say that I am personally disturbed about the way the United Nations and Mr. Hammarskjold as secretary-general have been carrying on negotiations, conversations and activities with respect to the situation in the Middle East. It would appear that the United Nations policy is made up of a series of curt orders to the friends of the western world, to those whom we call our allies, and a policy of appeasement and collaboration with Colonel Nasser of Egypt.

Supply-External Affairs
I would like to know what other nations are doing with regard to the request for assistance in the clearing of the canal. What is the Soviet union doing? What is India doing? What nations are participating in what we might call the preliminary advance for the purpose of clearing the canal? I think that information would be of assistance to us.
In conclusion I would like to pose a final question. On what is this advance being made? Is it an advance on a greater sum that we will be asked to contribute at a later date? I believe the Minister of Finance originally suggested it was a contribution and then he changed that expression and substituted the word "advance". He has suggested it is a loan. Well, just what is it? Is it, as I have already inquired, an advance on a larger contribution we will be asked to make at some future date? Will it be in the form of a loan? How will it be repaid and who is going to repay it? Someone has said it is just an item of $1 million. I suggest it is more than that because it relates to one of the greatest problems which confronts us at the present time.

Now, to go back over the other questions-

Mr. Chairman, the resolution has not been discussed before the United Nations. I would not be in a position either to say what the ultimate resolution would be or even to suggest the probability. I know a great many opinions have been expressed as to who might or might not be asked to pay for the cost, but at the present time I do not think any useful purpose would be served by our discussing that or expressing our own opinion at least for the time being.
The other discussions on this item ranged not only up and down the canal but off on to the mainland. I did not want to interrupt the Leader of the Opposition to suggest that he was not in order when he was speaking of the Gaza strip and other aspects of the current dispute between Israel and the Arab countries. However, I would not want to pass over any of the remarks he has made without some very brief reference to every matter he mentioned, although I think we ought to confine the discussion to the canal as such and the clearing thereof.
I think our position with respect to the Gaza strip is quite simple. Eight years ago the United Nations established certain armistice lines which brought to an end the hostilities which were then proceeding. Since that time everyone has recognized that a political solution to all the problems in the Middle East and in particular the dispute over Israel is highly desirable. I am sure that everyone in Canada would feel that if the United Nations could bring out of its present meeting or even out of protracted negotiations

Supply-External Affairs
over several months solutions which have not been attempted in some parts at all during the eight years, then a contribution of that kind and a good deal more might be justified. Peace in the Middle East, in my view and I think in the view of the government of Canada, depends on getting a political solution to these things which have been left in an uncertain state since 1948.
There is no question in my mind about the view the people of Canada would take about that settlement and that it ought to result in a recognition of the state of Israel by the Arab countries surrounding that state. We then ought to go ahead with our economic life without all the great expense to which all those countries have been put over the years in maintaining military establishments and thereby draining what might be a prosperous world of some of its means for improving the standard of living of the people.
The Gaza strip is not an issue in the vote before us. I can only say that we recognize it is one of the more current difficulties and it is hoped that the present negotiations going on at the United Nations will find some means of assuring that there will not be any form of chaos or lack of authority in that area during the course of the negotiations which might extend for some months.
The Leader of the Opposition has asked me to assure the committee that Nasser will be a law-abiding member of the United Nations. I am afraid that I am not in a position to sign any note of that kind.

It would be our desire that every member of the United Nations would be a law-abiding member thereof, but I do not think I should be expected to give any assurance of that kind. I do want to give the assurance that coupled with the vote of $1 million which I hope the committee will approve we will reiterate the position we have always taken on this matter, that is that the Suez canal shall be free to everyone without discrimination in its use. What form the operative part would take is still a matter of great concern and indeed may not be foreseen at the present time, but the United Nations resolution saying that this waterway shall be open to all users is not only endorsed by Canada but will be endorsed by Canada and insisted upon in so far as we have the ability to do so.
I do not think that I can answer in particular detail many of the other questions that have been asked. There was one question directly affecting the money side which I might refer to briefly. The Leader of the Opposition wanted to know if there was to be an apportionment of the responsibility. He wanted to know also why it was that we were called upon, to use his own words, to make a disproportionately large contribution to the present financing. I think that is what he had in mind. If I have not explained that clearly I will repeat.
The appeal for immediate funds was made to those countries which in the opinion of the secretary general could most easily, both financially and legislatively, provide the money at the earliest possible moment. We recognize that one in ten is a larger contribution than we are called upon to make in almost any other phase of the United Nations. In most cases our percentage contribution is less. But it is for the very reason that this is not an assessment but rather merely an appeal for funds that the amount we are presently asking parliament to vote is larger than we would normally be expected to give.
I think the Leader of the Opposition also wanted me to say something about certain guarantees which were made back in 1951. All I can add to what I have said already is that I would hope that out of the present session of the United Nations will come an acceptatfle solution or at least some method of determining an acceptable solution which might not be precisely in the form of the guarantees of 1951 or those of 1948 but which would nevertheless be a means whereby these difficulties along the Israeli and Egyptian borders could be resolved.
Under these circumstances I regret that I cannot go further. I do appreciate the remarks that have been made by all speakers, each one of whom I think has admitted that we ought to do this, and that the economic advantage in clearing the canal and having trade resumed and costs reduced in Europe, in fact in Asia and all shipping countries, would be of great advantage and would be a real contribution to the resumption, not only of normal trade but of that feeling which gives rise in some cases to political settlements which otherwise would not be so easily reached. If I have omitted anything I shall be glad to attempt to answer what I have missed.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Finance has treated this question as though everything were lovely and there were no obstacles in the way of success. He implied that it was just a matter of a little persuasion and a little bit of delay until the canal is opened again and all the trouble would be at an end. In the meantime Canada is going to pass out a mere million dollars to bring about this result. One might almost be excused for thinking the ministers were putting up this million dollars themselves. That seems the attitude of the Canadian representatives on this question, they make big fellows of themselves by having Canada contribute what is obviously an amount far in excess of what she should contribute.

speechtext:
Oh, "asking parliament to do it". There is no doubt about what the members sitting behind the minister and supporting him on this side of the house will do. The responsibility goes right back to the cabinet. Canada is advancing far more than her proper share, and I repeat that in effect the ministers are making good fellows of themselves at the expense of the Canadian taxpayer. This situation is just not as simple as the minister has made it appear.
I have here an extract from the U.S. News and World Report of January 25, 1957, which has this to say with regard to the situation in Suez:
In that Middle East tangle, here are things to keep an eye on: Suez canal clearance is to be far enough along in March to let some ships through. One issue is whether Nasser will let British, French, Israeli ships go through.
Obviously that has not been settled yet. The minister said this afternoon that the government of Canada would press for the free use of the canal by all nations, but it is perfectly clear that this man Nasser has not yet agreed to that; in fact he has been making threats that if certain conditions are hot adhered to, British, French and Israeli ships will not be allowed to use the canal. The dispatch in the V.S. News goes on:
Another Issue: will tolls be paid to Nasser? Test may come with the first ship to try transit. The west is getting braced for this test. Price of clearing canal remains to be settled. U.S. has advanced $5 million. Others have hung back. Who will pay, and how much, are the questions. U.N. police force may have to take on more jobs. It may be asked to police Gaza strip and gulf of Aqaba. Israel now holds these strategic areas. Egypt claims them. U.N. will have its hands full with this dispute.
This house should be told what stand Canada is to take with regard to Egypt paying something toward the clearing of the canal. After all, who was it blocked the canal in the most malicious piece of sabotage in many years? Egypt deliberately blocked this canal, with the result that it will cost somewhere around $30 million or $40 million to clear it. However, there was hot one word from the government today to suggest that they believe Egypt should pay at least some of this amount, not a breath of any such suggestion. Canada is rustling around and raising $1 million. The Americans are putting in $5 million, and they should put up 15 times as much as Canada. There is no reason why we should pay one-fifth as much as the Americans for this or any other similar project.
Nasser, the man who has brought about most of this trouble by breaking his agree-
Supply-External Affairs ments and by flouting the resolutions of the United Nations through the months and the years, is to get off scot-free, while the people of Canada are being asked to pay the shot. That is exactly what I said would happen when I spoke during the session last November. It is perfectly clear that we have now reached that situation, and I think instead of the minister getting up in a wishy-washy way and trying to get this vote through on soapsuds, a representative of the government should get up and say exactly what Canada believes should be done; and it should be insisted that this man Nasser should pay at least a reasonable proportion of the cost of clearing the canal. It is all very well to expect the people to pay and pay and pay, regardless of who is at fault.
In this whole deal it seems that the democratic countries, the ones that will follow the rules laid down by the United Nations, are those who will get all the abuse and all the insults, and then have to pay the shot. That is the position we are facing in this parliament today; a few words of maudlin sympathy for Israel, while at New York the Canadian representative is insisting that Israel must get out of the Gaza strip and away from the gulf of Aqaba before anything can be done. Could there be any situation more ridiculous?
I come now to another point. I ask the Minister of Finance or the Prime Minister to give the house some definite assurance with regard to what is to happen to this United Nations emergency force. There is a statement in the press this morning. One thing about these dictators-Hitler was the same, an'd Mussolini was the same-they always tell us exactly what they are going to do, and we never believe them; we always think it is too bad to be true, and we bury our heads in the sand. Then we wake up to the fact that they have actually done what they said they were going to do. Here is what appeared in the press this morning under the heading, "UNEF Won't Stay".
Cairo-Deputy foreign minister Fattah Hassan-
He is an official of the Egyptian government.
-said in an interview that "the United Nations emergency force will not remain in Egypt after Israel has withdrawn from Egyptian territory". In the interview, published in the newspaper A1 Massaa, he said: "UNEF will not remain in Egypt after completion of the mission entrusted by the United Nations regarding the withdrawal of all aggressors behind the armistice lines."
They have taken that stand from the start and the democratic nations have given in all the way through. We were led to believe when this force was first raised that it would be kept largely in the Suez canal area in order to see that there was free transit through

Supply-External Affairs the canal. We thought that the force was to act to bring about a final settlement of the question. But right through the piece Nasser has got everything he wished. He said that he would not have the force in the canal area and the troops had to go out into the Sinai desert. That is where they are now. He said he would not have the Queen's Own Rifles in Egypt and the Queen's Own Rifles went back to Calgary from Halifax, with alibis made by the Canadian Prime Minister and other members of the cabinet.
In the order in council passed on November 20, 1956, authorizing the sending of Canadian troops we find this paragraph:
And whereas member nations were invited to contribute self-contained battalion groups to which Canada agreed, as a result of which preparations were made to assemble such a force for dispatch in part by air and in part by H.M.C.S. Magnificent;
And so on. It was battalion groups that the United Nations wanted, but Nasser said there were not going to be any Canadian infantry troops and they were not sent. Every step has been dictated by Nasser. I think we are entitled to know now just what Canada is going to insist upon with regard to the United Nations emergency force. Is that force to remain in the Middle East until there has been a settlement of the boundary dispute between Israel and the Arab nations? Is it to go into the Gaza strip? Is it to go to the gulf of Aqaba? Is it to have any responsibility in the Suez canal area?
These are the sort of things the house should be told. If that is not the intention, then it is perfectly obvious what will happen. Israel, by the force of opinion built up by the nations that are opposed to her and want to see her wiped out, will be forced to get out of the Gaza strip and the gulf of Aqaba area. Then, following the same course that has been followed right through, Nasser will demand that the United Nations emergency force be withdrawn. The same nations that have been demanding that Israel withdraw will then demand that the United Nations emergency force withdraw and Nasser will be in complete control, built up to a position of dominance in that area far greater than Mussolini or Hitler ever achieved and built up primarily by the backing of the democratic nations, including Canada.
If that is the position that is to come about and if the Canadian government is going to sit back, do nothing about it and just let things drift, I suggest it will be a great tragedy. It will be out of line with the whole character and background of the Canadian people. The Canadian people are people who make their position known. They believe in taking a stand and making their

position known. I am sure they are not behind the government in the pussy-footing on this question, their policy of hanging back and trusting that everything will work out in the long run.
The Minister of Finance has not been able to give us any definite assurances, and I hope the Prime Minister of this country will rise from his seat this afternoon and assure the house and the country that Canada is going to take a determined stand to see that Nasser is not allowed to get away with any more of these dictatorial moves. Canada has taken a very large part in the United Nations emergency force, a part far in excess of what she was obliged to do. About one fifth of the troops in the force are from Canada even though none of them are infantry troops. I hope the Prime Minister will make it clear that Canada is going to insist that the United Nations emergency force remain in the Middle East until the question of boundaries has been finally settled and until free use of the Suez canal has been assured to all nations of the world.

The other day I asked a question on the orders of the day and I was not able to get any information at all. Mr. Chairman, what is happening in the Middle East today is almost a rewritten version of the retreats that were taken in 1936 in the league of nations and which ultimately and inevitably led to war. There is nothing more serious that can come before this parliament than a matter such as this. Nasser has simply defied everyone. He has defied the United Nations. He has laid down the terms. He has said, "These are the terms upon which a police force will operate against me". We ask what stand Canada is going to take. Mr. Chairman, I think that without infringing the very wise interpretation of the rule you have stated it is probably possible to say why this vote is being recommended to the Canadian parliament. There was a resolution adopted, in which Canada participated with a large number of other members, giving authority to the secretary general of the United Nations to proceed as expeditiously as possible in organizing the work of clearing the canal. In doing that he made commitments, on behalf of the United Nations, to those who have been doing very efficient work up to the present time in clearing the canal.
This being the case, we thought that we should continue to lend our support to the conduct of the secretary general in trying to bring about a settlement of the mid-eastern problem in a manner that would avoid the outbreak of war again in that region. It is because we still have confidence in the efforts that are being made to that end by the secretary general that we decided to recommend to parliament that this advance of $1 million be made as an advance without any commitment as to who should ultimately have to pay the cost of that necessary job, or the job that seemed to us to be necessary, and bring about a situation where a political settlement would not go back to the situation prior to last October, but would be a situation that would make for peace in the area with some reasonable assurance of permanency. It therefore is not foreign to the reasons for recommending this vote to the house to envisage the possibility of this being helpful to the realization of the objectives of so many of the members of the United Nations.
Now, the stand that was taken yesterday by the Secretary of State for External Affairs on behalf of Canada was that, under the terms of the resolution that had been adopted, priority was to be given to the withdrawal from the areas that had been-I do not want to use the word in a sense that would imply blame in any way-occupied by Israeli troops. It was felt that was not enough to comply with the real effect of the resolution that had been adopted; it was not enough to bring about a situation that would be merely the restoration of what took place before the occupation of those areas by Israeli troops, but it had to be something that would prevent those areas from being used again for the threats to Israel to which they amounted, and the raids that were being manned from those areas. It was felt that was something that must be considered at the same time as the general assembly was considering the report made by the secretary general that Israeli troops had not made a withdrawal

Supply-External Affairs from the Gaza strip or from the shores of Aqaba; that possibly as a matter of the right priority the withdrawal should be required first but should be accompanied by measures that would assure that there would not be merely the restoration of the preoccupation condition, but that there would be such measures as would provide for the security of Israel in respect of the raids which formerly had been launched from the Gaza strip or the Sinai desert and also the assurance of free passage through the canal to all shipping. That is the theme which the Secretary of State for External Affairs developed in his speech yesterday and the hon. gentleman will see in some of the headlines in the Ottawa newspapers tonight that there is very substantial support for the attitude taken by the Secretary of State for External Affairs in that speech of yesterday morning.
The resolution that will follow is now being discussed. The hon. gentleman knows, as I do, that whatever we may feel our position to be, Canada cannot dictate what the resolutions adopted by the general assembly will be. There has to be an affirmative vote of two-thirds of the membership to carry a resolution and we know, and I am sure the hon. gentleman knows, that many discussions are taking place at this time between these various delegations to get the kind of resolution that will conform with the position expressed in the speech of the Secretary of State for External Affairs yesterday morning, and that will have the support of a two-thirds majority and that will reassert the statement that the Israeli troops should withdraw, but will be accompanied by further statements that immediately following the withdrawal such and such dispositions will be taken to prevent the situation from remaining no better than it was before the occupation of those areas.
The suggestion is being made in strong terms by a number of delegations that the United Nations emergency force should police that whole area for such period as might give time to bring about a settlement that will make for-I perhaps should not say permanent peace in the area but will make for stability-and for the removal of the Immediate threats of the resumption of hostilities.

for the resumption of hostilities. It is because we feel that the resumption of hostilities would be disturbing to the whole world including Canada that the Secretary of State for External Affairs is doing his best, as are many others, to bring about a situation where security can be achieved without a resumption of hostilities, and that can be achieved along the lines he has stated, the security of Israel against the raids that came from that area and the right of all nations to make use of the canal.
As to what will be the ultimate way in which the funds will be raised: Will it be an assessment against the members of the United Nations? That has been suggested and it does not seem to have very strong prospects of being the solution adopted. Another solution is extra or supplemental tolls paid by the users of the canal to provide through those supplemental tolls the amount that will have been expended to clear the canal and to make it open for shipping generally. These things cannot be brought to a head quickly. It has always been our experience in drafting, when several are concerned that not every mind envisages the proper way to express the proper ideas in the same fashion and in the same language, and these things take time. When you have to have two-thirds of 80 in favour in order to get an effective resolution, it takes some time and some negotiation to have them all agree that the proper words, the proper punctuation and the proper order of expressing the decisions are contained in the document submitted. That is work with respect to which the Secretary of State for External Affairs has had quite a lot of experience. I am not asking hon. members opposite to share that admiration but I know the Secretary of State for External Affairs has won much admiration from other delegations at the United Nations for what he has been able to do in that respect. To make a positive statement and say, "It must be this or we are not going to support it," is not apt to bring about the adoption of a resolution supported by a two-thirds majority of the 80 members of the assembly. That is the situation as it stands at the present time and I hope it will mature into a resolution that will have the required support from many quarters. I appreciate, of course, that it is rather unpalatable for hon. members of this house to have to learn what is being said or done elsewhere but it must be realized that it is the "elsewhere" that is the forum where the resolutions are going to be discussed and adopted.

I think the hon. gentleman will recognize that what I am saying will accord with what he himself has observed on more than one occasion when he has visited the assembly halls either of the security council or of the general assembly of the United Nations. The government is not in the same position in the United Nations as it is in the Canadian parliament. In the Canadian parliament it can put forward its proposal and if the proposal is not adopted the government stands defeated and another government is called in to take its place. At the United Nations that is not the situation. If the Canadian delegation takes a stand as an unalterable stand and it is not acceptable to a majority of two-thirds of the 80 members of the United Nations, the resolution is just not adopted. Under present conditions I think it would be a very sorry result for the United Nations. I hope hon. members will feel, as I do, that if this situation can be cleared up in a satisfactory way through the actions of the United Nations the prestige of that body will have been greatly enhanced and the confidence of the world at large in that body and its efficiency will have been greatly increased.
That is what we have been trying to do; that is what we have been trying to bring about. It is true that if this were to be a contribution or an assessment of what Canada might be expected to pay for the clearing of the Suez canal it would be out of proportion. It may be that our contribution to the United Nations force is out of proportion, but after all the general who has been chosen as the commander for the United Nations is a gentleman of Canadian citizenship for whom I think we all have admiration and whom we felt it would not be the desire of the Canadian people to let down in his efforts to discharge successfully the responsibilities that have been placed upon his shoulders by the United Nations. That is the reason this government has endeavoured to meet the requests made by General Bums as to the kind of assistance he would feel he should have from Canadian personnel with whom he was of course more familiar than he would be with personnel supplied by other nations. It was for that reason that there were these alterations made in the original plan. My hon. friends on the other side say that it is because it was at the dictation of Nasser.

referred continually to the fact that this idea was suggested by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. As I read the record, and as the Prime Minister now says, it was first advanced by Henry Cabot Lodge, the representative of the United States.
There is one thing that has not been cleared up by the answer given by the Prime Minister. The secretary general of the United Nations appears to be under the impression that his mandate does not go beyond directing Israel to remove its forces. It does not permit him to suggest any further action that should be taken in order to maintain the integrity of Israel and preserve the Suez canal for the use of all nations.
Over and over again he has taken the stand that Nasser has to consent. Up to the present time Nasser has certainly dictated the course which has been followed. He says: These are the rules; this is the kind of force I will accept; these are the terms under which that force will operate. For any nations of the free world to accept his ipse dixit as the final decision and basis of settlement; for the nations to accept in their entirety his declarations may cause a temporary appeasement, but all history shows that those who thirst for blood are not appeased. In the speech yesterday by the Secretary of State for External Affairs these words appear:
3. Empower the secretary general to deploy the emergency force into the vital areas as Israel pulls out-hut to consult both disputants before making such a move. The force thus would take over the duties of the old UN Palestine truce team but would extend them along the Aqaba gulf coast.
Now, I ask the Prime Minister this. Do the consultations which are being carried on with the disputants imply that both the disputants must consent to the force being used? Up to the present time Mr. Hammarskjold has taken a very firm stand that no action anticipated to be taken on Egyptian soil shall be taken without the consent of the government of Egypt. The Gaza area and part of the area on the gulf of Aqaba have been accepted as


Egyptian territory since 1948. Will it be necessary to have Nasser's consent as a condition for the moving in of the United Nations emergency force to patrol those areas? If it will not, I think the general plan will meet with universal approval of the people of this country, because that is what has been asked for; it is reasonable, and it is the only way in which there is any possibility of preserving peace in the Middle East.
On the other hand, if the means to be taken have to be acceptable to Nasser then those means cannot achieve peace. They may result in the continuance of a truce, or of an armistice, but there can be no peace in following the dictated determinations of Nasser. I therefore ask the Prime Minister this. Is it intended that the emergency force or the United Nations force, the truce administration or whatever you like to call it, will move in and will not require the consent of Nasser before doing so?

speechtext: I think this is a matter of semantics rather than a matter of politics. "Will they require the consent of Nasser to move in?" They will require that there be no armed opposition to their moving in, and that is in accord with what has been the pursuit of the United Nations since it was seized with this problem of bringing about a settlement that would not require force of arms for its achievement. It is not only the force of arms that acts upon the acquiescence of parties to a dispute. If the hon. gentleman will read the whole of the speech made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs he will see that there is a dispute as to the legal situation with respect to the Gaza strip and the Aqaba shores, and the minister for external affairs recommends that the question be submitted to the international court for adjudication but that in the meantime both parties give assurances that there will be no attempt to make use of these areas for the resumption of active hostilities.

The emergency force will be there to see to it that there is no resort to a resumption of armed hostilities.
The whole affair is very much made up of different scenes, if you will, of the same drama; and it is for that reason, Mr. Chairman, that I have ventured to mention things that do not deal obviously and directly with the recommendation of this vote to the House of Commons. This is only one of the scenes of the drama, and the main actors are not always those who first appear upon the public

stage. The hon. gentleman says the first public suggestion of this procedure was made by Hr. Lodge, and that is quite true. But the hon. gentleman also knows that there had been discussions behind the scenes for several days, and those discussions dealt not only with what should be proposed but also with who should make the proposals, so as to ensure that they might receive the widest possible acceptance.
The hon. gentleman knows, as I do, that the sponsorship of resolutions is frequently a matter which requires a great deal of discussion behind the scenes before it is agreed upon, and even now I hope the representative of India will find it possible to join in sponsorship of the resolutions that will be brought forward. I know there may be some wishful thinking with regard to that, but the hon. gentleman will see in the dispatches that a resolution is very apt to come about as something arising out of the atmosphere that develops, or will develop, among the delegations during this adjournment.
I do not think the hon. gentleman would imagine, and neither do I, that there were no resolutions ready when the adjournment was suggested, but it was felt that before bringing these forward it would be better to have this adjournment so they could be discussed in a forum where no one was taking a public stand from which a retreat would have involved loss of face.
I for my part-and my colleagues feel as I do-trust a great deal in the discretion and tact of our Secretary of State for External Affairs in the manoeuvres to which resort must be had in order to bring about something that proves acceptable to a two-thirds majority of the general assembly.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO INTRODUCTION OF FURTHER LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a word or two about the purpose of this proposed loan of $1 million to the United Nations; and by way of introducing the remarks I wish to make, may I say I believe it is the common belief of the house that we are now being asked to vote this sum because of some prior action taken by the government of Canada.
We were here in November, when we debated at some length an action which was then fresh in our minds and which had just been instituted in the United Nations. I, for one, though regarding it hopefully and supporting the vote that was taken at that time in respect of the United Nations emergency force, raised some very serious questions and doubts which everyone must have had regarding the choice the Canadian government, along with other countries, made to remove the police action in the area from the
Supply-External Affairs hands of the French and British and place it under the direction of the assembly of the United Nations. That choice was made and that again has gone on under the direction of the general assembly. Today, in consequence of that choice and action, we are now providing funds as a loan to pay for one of the objectives which the United Nations assembly is trying to attain.
I agree that it is not an easy problem. Everyone here will agree that to lend $1 million to clear the Suez canal for traffic and, more important, to re-establish it as a channel of free international trade, is a worthy objective, and I am sure the government will secure the necessary vote. But the fact that we are voting the money, the fact that the government will have the money in its hands and will lend it and will be under responsibility to the house and the country to account for the expenditure and demonstrate as time goes on that the expenditure has produced a result that is worth while, also brings into issue the initial choice the government made in sponsoring in the United Nations the resolution to set up the emergency force. It also brings into issue the government's conduct in pursuing that choice at the United Nations, as our Secretary of State for External Affairs is doing at this very moment.
The Prime Minister raised the difficulty which we all see of obtaining a two-thirds majority. That must have been in the minds of the government when they undertook the course they are now following and undertook to put the responsibility for the solution of the Middle East problem in the hands of the assembly.
It is quite true that a two-thirds majority is needed for every resolution, that the assembly can only act by resolution, and that if that majority cannot be obtained the whole procedure, the whole course of this remedy, this police action, this attempt to solve the present issues in the Middle East, may be completely stultified. But that is something upon which the government has entered with its eyes open and knowing the consequences of using the general assembly for that purpose. We said at the time, and I repeat, that we were hopeful the choice made and the action we are taking today would lead to a more effective means of dealing with this kind of international problem where some exercise of authority, either by states in association or by the United Nations through an emergency force, is absolutely essential to the correction of disorder and to the correction of those who create the disorders.
I say we are hopeful it will lead to something, but let me say this, and this is the point I wish to make. The government has

Supply-External Affairs made a choice which has resulted in the action under way today, and the government is on trial in carrying through the consequences of that choice in the general assembly of the United Nations. The people of Canada will look to them to justify their conduct by success. Therefore what we have to see to in voting funds, and all we can see to, is that the government will not be content with anything less than the objective which has been so well stated today, a solution of these problems through action of the United Nations, a solution which does not depend on the consent of one of the parties, the consent of Nasser of Egypt or any consent which will nullify the solution of the three important problems respecting the Suez, the Israeli-Arab dispute and the question of the Arab refugees.
The latter two are not in dispute today, but the disposition of the canal problem is the object of this vote. I do suggest that the money will be wasted and the course of the government's action will be condemned in time by the people of the country unless they take a firm line at the United Nations and justify the choice they made some months ago. That can only be done by being insistent and convincing. The Secretary of State for External Affairs is a very tactful and convincing man. We hope he will succeed and that the general assembly will be effective in solving the problem. As I say, the government is on trial, the minister is on trial, and we are looking to them to justify the course which has been taken.

speechtext:
We are voting here $1 million, a considerable sum of money; and in the light of the explanation advanced, part of which was conveyed to me at secondhand because it was necessary for me to be out of the house earlier this afternoon, it seems to me that many of the essential elements have not been fully explained. This item appears under a rather unusual heading, namely "Loans, Investments and Advances". As I understand it, a loan is something, usually money, that is given with the understanding that it will be returned. An investment is something into which you put your money in the hope that it will appreciate and bring some sort of return. An advance is a going forward.

I do not think it has been explained how the loan is to be secured. Originally there was a reported though not confirmed proposal put forward by some United States bankers under which they would advance to the United Nations the full amount of the money, not only the $10 million but the total sum of $50 million required to clear the canal. I understand that from their investigations they were not satisfied that there would be any enforceable obligation on the United Nations whereby that body would have to repay the money. That opinion was obtained by people in the investment business, but even in the face of that the representation is made to the house that this amount is in the nature of a loan and is an amount of money that will be returned. I think the Minister of Finance should assure us that there is an enforceable obligation under which the money will be repaid if the amount is in fact a loan. If it is a gift then the item should be clothed in the proper language and so described.
There is another thing I think we might reasonably consider. International loans generally bear interest. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation says that when the Canadian people borrow money for housing they must pay 6 per cent. There is no suggestion here that the Canadian people as a whole in going into a foreign market with their money, if you like, are going to receive any return by way of interest.
I remember well the Prime Minister saying last session that the Suez was no concern of ours, that we did not have any ships going through the canal, and why should we bother with anything going on in that area. Looking at the item in a rather cold-blooded fashion, and that is the way I think the Minister of Finance should look at a financial transaction, I think he might give us some indication whether there is to be any financial return. I am sure it would be of interest to his department and the people of the country as a whole.
This afternoon the Prime Minister made certain references to an address by the Secretary of State for External Affairs to the United Nations. I thought it rather significant that he omitted any suggestion that the resolution proposed to the United Nations is not going to carry in its present form, and in all honesty I think it should have been said that it was not intended that it should carry in the form in which it was proposed. By the language used and by everything the Prime Minister said I think there is rather the suggestion that someone has come up with an answer. The Afro-Asian group will not subscribe to the proposal put forward by the Secretary of State

for External Affairs, and the Prime Minister well knows they will not.
Knowing that, I think he should go further and explain to us what steps Canada is taking in that regard. It is nice to refer to things that are to be done, but the motive behind the action should also be explained to this house. Let us go further and see what assurance can be taken from the assembly and what hope there is of ensuring the success of this assurance. How much more are we going to be asked for after this $1 million is spent? Is there then going to be another call made on the Canadian people? Can the Prime Minister assure us that all members of the United Nations are going to participate in this and that if the secretary general does reach some formula, all nations are going to support it? Or is this just $1 million tossed out in hope? If that is the situation, let us hear it.
As I recall it, I do not think any of the eastern countries have yet agreed, either by resolution, speech, communication or in any other way, that they are willing to participate in any United Nations levy in order to repay any money used in clearing the Suez canal. If that is the situation I think, with the greater facilities available to this government, we should be informed about this matter. Do not put something forward and then say, "Now pass it". We feel that we should hear who is going to be responsible for the repayment of this loan; whether all the members of the United Nations have agreed to subscribe to the formula that the secretary general may produce, and also whether there is any term on the loan and whether we have any assurance as to when, if ever, it will be repaid.
