speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in the course of the Prime Minister's remarks he said something about people hoping that the emergency force now stationed in the Middle East could prevent an outbreak of hostilities. I do not see that the present emergency force, being a lightly armed infantry force, could do anything to stop the opposing forces of Israel or Egypt if those two countries decided to engage in hostilities again, because those hostilities would be undertaken by armour, aeroplane and heavy equipment. The emergency force, I think in the words of the secretary general himself, is only an enlarged observer corps. The prevention of an outbreak of hostilities-and everyone is fervently hoping that such an outbreak will not occur-must be accomplished by other means.
Earlier the Prime Minister, in speaking of this loan which is for the clearing of the canal, indicated that it was one of the steps
Supply-External Affairs toward reaching a political settlement in the Middle East. He said, and I hope I copied down his words correctly, that it would be helpful to a realization of the objectives of so many members of the United Nations. It is in that light that we are considering this matter. If this is to be helpful to a realization of the objectives of members of the United Nations, we must be clear in our minds as to what those objectives are.
Mainly, of course, the objective is to ensure that there will not be an outbreak of hostilities in the Middle East, and that Israel and Egypt will not again enter upon war. But over the last eight years armed conflict of a sort has been going on between Egypt and Israel, with border raids and things of that nature. Resolutions of the United Nations have been ignored quite frequently by both sides. Certainly one of the great difficulties that Israel was experiencing with Egypt was the denial of passage through the canal to ships carrying the Israeli flag, and the prevention of ships destined for Israel from reaching the port at the top of the gulf of Aqaba. Unless that main problem is resolved, how can a cessation of hostilities between those two countries be assured?
At the present moment the United Nations is considering the problem and the Canadian representative has, according to the Ottawa Citizen, about to be presented to the United Nations a resolution which must be split into two parts now if there is any hope at all of having it passed. In today's issue of the Citizen it is stated:
. . . Canada and a number of other nations will introduce two resolutions later this week-
That is to be done in order to get over this difficulty of the one draft resolution of Canada, which apparently is not acceptable.
-the first reiterating the U.N. demand that Israel withdraw its troops from Gaza and the Aqaba gulf area and the second ordering immediate efforts to expand the role of the U.N. emergency force in maintaining an armistice on the Egyptian-Israeli border.
The difficulty is that those nations that are opposed to Israel are insisting that Israel withdraw her troops completely before any further action is taken. Yet unless further action is taken, what is the situation? Here is what the Secretary of State for External Affairs said in the assembly debate, and this is within quotation marks in the newspaper. He was speaking about the situation that would result if there was any possibility of failure to pass the second resolution, namely the one to use the emergency force in those

Supply-External Affairs areas and on the Egyptian-Israeli border. If there is a failure there, he says, this will be the situation:
. . . this failure "will be a demonstration of the futility of this organization (the U.N.) that would have devastating effects" on world affairs.
Then he went on to say this, and this is summarized in the paper; these are not his direct words:
The Israelis would stay put; the Arabs would try to level sanctions on Israel through the U.N.; new outbreaks of violence might take place; soon the UNEF would be forced out of the Middle East and a novel international experiment killed.
Hence it all rests on an "if", Mr. Chairman, if the second proposed draft resolution is passed. If it is not passed, then there is the quandary. If the first one is passed and is agreed to by Israel, the Gaza strip will be evacuated of Israeli troops, the Aqaba gulf area will be cleared of Israeli troops, and the emergency force at that stage is not moving in. Unless it moves in the Egyptian forces will move in, and there will be a situation such as that which prevailed during the last eight years. Hence unless this second draft resolution passes the assembly, which resolution refers to the utilization of the emergency force, we will have achieved no solution to the problem in the Middle East.
It is quite obvious that the second draft resolution should have priority and should be passed before insistence is directed to Israel to withdraw her troops. Canada's position, which is being made a little bit clearer day by day and as this debate continues, seems not to have been very strong. It rests upon too many suppositions as to what might happen if something else is done. I would have preferred an insistence by Canada on a reversal of this order and the proper use of the emergency forces in these two disputed areas. If Canada is going to go along with these other nations and insist that Israel withdraw completely and then merely take a chance on the emergency force being used, I think we are in a very difficult position.
If the use of the emergency force depends, in the last analysis, on the consent of Nasser, experience in the past shows that such consent will not be forthcoming. To what has Nasser consented up to the moment? I do not know of any resolution of the United Nations to which he has given consent, unless he drafted the resolution himself and had it presented in a form that would be acceptable to him. What confidence can we place in any of these resolutions being accepted by Nasser? The situation, therefore, becomes even more involved and Canada's position should be made much clearer; that we stand firm on


the use of the emergency force, that novel international experiment. It was that with which we went along in the early part of December, a trial run of this international experiment, the use of an emergency force so that peace would prevail in a sensitive area of the world and so that during the period of peace a permanent political settlement might be made.
But this novel international experiment, in the opinion of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, is very close to being a failure because of the grave difficulty in the United Nations at the present time as to how this force shall be used. Of course, back of it all is the yielding to Nasser's demands right from the end of October to the present day. A firm stand against Nasser should have been taken much earlier. Canada's offer to send the Queen's Own, rejected by Nasser, was an indication that there would be trouble in persuading the Egyptian dictator to do anything that might be asked of him by the United Nations. So the United Nations faces, I suppose, the most perilous moment in its history, and we are intensely interested in Canada's actions and activities under those circumstances.
It is for this reason that I think it would have been better if, earlier this afternoon, there had been a full disclosure by the government as to the instructions that had been given to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. The Prime Minister seemed to imply, when he was speaking this afternoon, that the Secretary of State for External Affairs, in speaking yesterday to the assembly, had outlined the stand of the government of Canada. I would have liked to interrupt to ask the Prime Minister if he could not inform the house as to the instructions that had been given the minister prior to the delivery of that speech yesterday. This would have been helpful, rather than compelling us to go through a process of endeavouring to extract information from a reluctant government. The situation is much too serious for anything in the nature of failure to provide complete information.
If hostilities break out in the Middle East, immediately a thousand-odd Canadian soldiers are in danger. It was our interest in the safety of those soldiers that caused us on this side of the house to ask where they were located. I think we require even more information with regard to the protection that is afforded, particularly the Canadian troops who are the administration echelon of the emergency force. Are they in an exposed position? Are they protected by the infantry battalions that have been supplied by other

nations, or might they be unhappily sacrificed in any outbreak of hostilities? This concern must be in the minds of the Canadian people, and is certainly in the minds of the relatives of our soldiers who are overseas.
Under those circumstances we cannot, without careful consideration, enter into the voting of a million dollars to assist Nasser in clearing the canal which he blocked after the outbreak of hostilities, the canal from which he perhaps intends to derive a great deal of revenue. Why should we, without guarantees concerning the future, be so quick to assist Nasser in re-establishing his economic position in respect of the canal? Let us hear from him or from the proper sources as to
Supply-External Affairs what he intends to do to ensure that after clearance of the canal, assisted by our money, it will be free to international traffic without any hindrance whatever; that it will be free to the ships of Israel, and that the ships of Britain and France will not be prevented from making use of it. None of these assurances have been given, and something in the way of a definite assurance is required before we should be asked to vote such a large sum.
I see that it is six o'clock, Mr. Chairman.
Progress reported.
At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
